title: The Big Studios
objective: After this level you can explain why the major studios owned the whole chain, from making films to the theaters that showed them.
summary: By 1930 eight studios made 95 percent of American films. The five majors owned the whole chain, from production to theaters, and block booking pushed their films into the rest.

cards.headline: What if a bakery owned every café that sold its bread?
cards.body: It would never worry about shelf space. Hollywood's biggest studios worked like that: they made films, rented them out to theaters and owned many of the theaters that showed them. Why would a movie studio want to own the whole chain?

cards.headline: Five majors, three minors
cards.body: By 1930, eight studios made 95 percent of American films. Five majors, MGM, Paramount, Warner Brothers, Twentieth Century-Fox and RKO, controlled all three links: production (making films), distribution (renting them to theaters) and exhibition (showing them). Universal, Columbia and United Artists made and distributed films but didn't own the big theater chains.
cards.callout: Make it · Ship it · Show it

cards.headline: Why buy the theaters?
cards.body: Through the 1920s, Paramount, MGM and other studios bought up chains of first-run theaters. After that, Britannica says, the majors are best seen as theater chains that made features, shorts, cartoons and newsreels to fill their own houses. Owning the screens meant every film a studio made had a place to play.

mascot.line: Keep this: the majors didn't just make movies. They owned the rooms where you watched them.

cards.headline: Films sold by the block
cards.body: Theaters the studios didn't own still needed their films, and the studios set the terms. Under block booking, a theater could license the film it wanted only if it also took other films the distributor released in that period. Want this season's big picture? Take the package.

cards.headline: The big studios: mapped
learned: By 1930, eight studios made 95 percent of American films
Five majors made, distributed and showed films
They bought theater chains to fill with their own films
Block booking: take the package to get the film

questions.prompt: Under block booking, a theater that wanted one film had to _____.

options.label: buy shares in the studio
options.rationale: Block booking was about licensing films, not shares.

options.label: show it only on weekends
options.rationale: It set which films came in the deal, not when they played.

options.label: pay the studio's actors
options.rationale: Theaters dealt with distributors, not actors.

questions.explanation: Block booking licensed a film only on condition that the theater also took other films released by that distributor in the same period.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the studio business with what it means.
questions.explanation: Production is making films, distribution is renting them to theaters, and exhibition is showing them. Under block booking, a theater that wanted the big picture had to take the package.

questions.prompt: In Level 5, projection beat the peep show because one screen served many paying viewers. How did the 1930s majors push that logic further?

options.label: They went back to one-viewer cabinets
options.rationale: They stuck with projection, and owned the rooms.

options.label: They stopped renting films to other theaters
options.rationale: They still rented films out, often by the block.

options.label: They owned the theaters with those screens, too
They let audiences in for free
options.rationale: Ticket sales were the whole point.

questions.explanation: Projection made one screen pay for many viewers. The majors went a step further and owned the screens, controlling production, distribution and exhibition.
